tl;dr - I'm proposing changing UnboundedOperator from a structure extending LinearPMap to a prop on LinearPMaps to make sums/compositions easier.

In working with unbounded operators I am running up against some difficulties having to do with algebraic properties and sums.
Here is the current definition (see previous discussion):

/-- An `UnboundedOperator` is a linear map from a submodule of `H` to `H'`,
  assumed to be both densely defined and closable. -/
structure UnboundedOperator
    (H : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H] [CompleteSpace H]
    (H' : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup H'] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H'] [CompleteSpace H']
    extends LinearPMap ℂ H H' where
  /-- The domain of an unbounded operator is dense in `H`. -/
  dense_domain : Dense (domain : Set H)
  /-- An unbounded operator is closable. -/
  is_closable : toLinearPMap.IsClosable

The issue is that addition and composition of UnboundedOperators may result in LinearPMaps which are not densely defined or not closable. I had previously accounted for this by defining addition with some junk (zero) values when the sum is not an unbounded operator. However, I have recently realized that one cannot take finite sums (such as is needed for the kinetic energy operator, ∑ i : Fin d, (P i).comp (P i)) since this requires an AddCommMonoid structure that is not possible given that the junk values spoil add_assoc.

I think that life would be much cleaner if we shift to having UnboundedOperator as a property distinguishing special types of LinearPMaps.
Here is a MWE of my vision with some simple example lemmas:

import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.LinearPMap
open InnerProductSpace

variable
  (H : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H] [CompleteSpace H]
  (H' : Type*) [NormedAddCommGroup H'] [InnerProductSpace ℂ H'] [CompleteSpace H']

namespace LinearPMap

def HasDenseDomain (U : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H') : Prop := Dense (U.domain : Set H)

-- Note that we cannot simply co-opt `LinearMap.IsSymmetric` because the domain and codomain
-- may not be the same.
def IsSymmetric (T : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H) : Prop := ∀ x y : T.domain, ⟪T x, ↑y⟫_ℂ = ⟪↑x, T y⟫_ℂ

lemma HasDenseDomain.add_of_le
    {U U' : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H'} (h : U.HasDenseDomain) (h_le : U.domain ≤ U'.domain) :
    (U + U').HasDenseDomain :=
  Dense.mono (by simp [add_domain, h_le]) h

lemma isClosable_of_isSymmetric {T : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H} (h : T.IsSymmetric) (h' : T.HasDenseDomain) :
    T.IsClosable := by
  apply isClosable_iff_exists_closed_extension.mpr
  exact ⟨T†, adjoint_isClosed h', IsFormalAdjoint.le_adjoint h' h⟩

lemma IsSymmetric.add {T₁ T₂ : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H} (h₁ : T₁.IsSymmetric) (h₂ : T₂.IsSymmetric) :
    (T₁ + T₂).IsSymmetric := by
  intro x y
  specialize h₁ ⟨x, Set.mem_of_mem_inter_left x.2⟩ ⟨y, Set.mem_of_mem_inter_left y.2⟩
  specialize h₂ ⟨x, Set.mem_of_mem_inter_right x.2⟩ ⟨y, Set.mem_of_mem_inter_right y.2⟩
  simp_all [add_apply, inner_add_left, inner_add_right]

end LinearPMap

/-- An unbounded operator is a LinearPMap which is both densely defined and closable.
  Most operators encountered in physics satisfy these properties, most notably
  self-adjoint operators (observables). -/
def IsUnboundedOperator (U : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H') : Prop := U.HasDenseDomain ∧ U.IsClosable
-- or
def UnboundedOperator : Type _ := {U : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H' // U.HasDenseDomain ∧ U.IsClosable}

lemma IsUnboundedOperator.add_v1 {U U' : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H'} (h : U.IsUnboundedOperator)
    (h' : U'.IsUnboundedOperator) (hD : (U + U').HasDenseDomain)
    (h_bound : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ x : U.domain, ‖U x‖ ≤ C * ‖x‖) :
    (U + U').IsUnboundedOperator := by
  sorry

lemma IsUnboundedOperator.add_v2 {U U' : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H} (hD : (U + U').HasDenseDomain)
    (hS : U.IsSymmetric) (hS' : U'.IsSymmetric) :
    (U + U').IsUnboundedOperator :=
  ⟨hD, isClosable_of_isSymmetric (hS.add hS') hD⟩

A byproduct is that I think it makes the process of defining unbounded operators simpler. As it is, one must first define a LinearPMap, prove that it is dense/closable/symmetric and then using these define the corresponding UnboundedOperator (see physlib#1088 for a recent example). With the proposed change one would instead just have def myOperator : H →ₗ.[ℂ] H' := … and then prove myOperator.IsUnboundedOperator as a theorem with no auxiliary definitions needed.

I understand that structures are generally preferred but in this case I think they are actively getting in the way! I'd love to hear peoples' thoughts or suggestions on how to make things better.

I'm not against this, but I'm unsure what it actually gives you here because you (I think) always want to stay in the space of unbounded operators. All this seems to do is move the problem.

In particular, for the kinetic energy example, KT := ∑ i : Fin d, (P i).comp (P i), you really want this to be an unbounded operator (correct me if I'm wrong), so you either have to do: 

def KT : UnboundedOperator where
   toLinearPMap :=  ∑ i : Fin d, ((P i).comp (P i)). toLinearPMap
   dense_domain := proof
   is_closable := proof

or 

-- (P i) are LinearPMap here
def KT : LinearPMap :=  ∑ i : Fin d, ((P i).comp (P i))

lemma KT_isUnboundedOperator : IsUnboundedOperator KT := by
   constructor
   . proof
   . proof

In addition, (because you always want UnboundedOperators), you will end up having to keep inserting proofs of e.g. Adjoints of UnboundedOperators are UnboundedOperators etc.

Just some thoughts - there may be other benefits I'm not seeing here. In Mathlib I think there is precedence either way e.g. docs#ContinuousLinearMap and docs#Matrix.IsHermitian.

I have been actually thinking the same thing, so my short answer is IMO go for it and see what problems this method creates/solves and compare to the existing version.

The long answer is I think it's generally better to make definitions easy to write rather than nicely bundled. In the case that Joseph wrote where you're creating a named operator which you want to always be an unbounded operator, I agree the difference is nominal. But if you want to write just the sum ∑ i : Fin d, (P i).comp (P i) you can't do that if we're working in UnboundedOperator because Finset.sum requires AddCommMonoid which includes associativity - but we can write that in LinearPMap. I also think there will be situations where we may want to have unbounded operators f and g and it's still useful to say what f + g means even if the result isn't an unbounded operator. And in the case that f + g is unbounded you can then prove that using the properties of your specific operators f and g - or perhaps you have a situation where you only need dense domain or closable and not both.

I will also note that from my limited research it seems this isn't going to be resolved by picking a "better" junk value for addition, the blocker to associativity is inherent to the unboundedness condition.

Another thought I had was defining the type unbounded operators whose domain contains a particular dense subspace in which case I think the associativity problem goes away and in practice we usually have this situation. But I'd much prefer a more general framework and we can define this later using either general framework so there's not a good reason to limit ourselves.

This is my understanding as well.

defining the type unbounded operators whose domain contains a particular dense subspace in which case I think the associativity problem goes away and in practice we usually have this situation

This would definitely work to ensure sums remain densely defined, but I think closability remains an issue - one cannot have an AddCommMonoid structure because the sum of two closable operators defined on E being closable requires a proof. Limiting to symmetric operators with common domain E would work, but this seems far too restrictive.

I think I will go ahead with implementing this prop version to see if there are any unanticipated drawbacks and allow a side-by-side comparison. Here is what I expect:
Pros:

  • Better 'logic' in defining unbounded operators (as it stands the proofs of denseness/closability/symmetry can be long and are better established on some auxiliary LinearPMap before wrapping everything together).
  • Lemmas which don't rely on density or closability can be more general.

Cons:

  • Having to show IsUnboundedOperator is preserved when doing "simple" operations (smul, neg, adjoint).
  • Lose structure and ability to add instances in the future.

Mixed bag:

  • All of the algebraic structures (e.g. SubtractionCommMonoid, SemilatticeInf) would be free, but one would need to show how they interact with the IsUnboundedOperator property.

I've opened up physlib#1090 as a draft with the prop-based unbounded operators in a new file Unbounded_v2.lean - let me know what you think!
It remains to flesh out compositions / sums (e.g. for kinetic energy), but I am encouraged by how much shorter the file has become.
This looks good to me! Can you tag any of these propositions with @[fun_prop]? If so I think this would make your life a lot easier.
It looks like this isn't possible because LInearPMap is not of type α → β. I've just now checked LinearMap.IsSymmetric and the algebraic operations get @[aesop safe apply] tags instead.

Ok, that is a shame. I wonder how much the @[aesop safe apply] attribute is actually helpful to us in this case.

Unrelated to the above: Can most of the actual definitions on UnboundedOperator be extended to LinearPMap? I.e. do you think you will ever actually have to carry around the Is UnboundedOperator in definitions, or do you think it will only be needed in theorems?

For here: I think if we stick with this IsUnboundedOperator approach we should write about the two different implementations in the relevant doc-string and why the given approach is chosen.

I'm not sure what you mean by "definitions on UnboundedOperator" - can you give an example? But I think IsUnbounded would only show up in theorems, except maybe if it is convenient to define some subtype of LinearPMap consisting of symmetric/self-adjoint unbounded operators on a common domain.

I think you've answered my question here already, but by definitions on UnboundedOperator I just meant definitions which are of the form e.g. 

def adjoint (H : UnboundedOperator) : ... := ...

rather than extending too

def adjoint (H : LinearPMap) : ... := ...

(which e.g. the case of adjoint does).

Ah, I understand. Yes, with the new system all operations (add + assoc, smul + distrib, adjoint, closure, etc.) are on LinearPMaps and already defined in Mathlib.
This was part of my motivation to have IsUnbounded just as a prop with lemmas showing how it propagates.

I think I am happy with where the PR is now. This is quite the overhaul, so if everyone is on board with making this structural change I will work to split up the PR into a few more manageable pieces.

Gave review with minor suggestions on naming, and since this is starting to establish a naming convention I wanted to make note of it here:

One challenge with naming is that there are several iterations of maps corresponding to the same operation. This PR uses the convention that names for

  • LinearMaps end in LM
  • ContinuousLinearMaps end in CLM
  • LinearPMaps end in Operator
    So the partial linear maps are what we actually call operators and other maps are labeled by type name.

Additionally, name modifiers go at the end before the type name. So for example if the momentum operator is named momentumOperator the momentum squared operator is momentumSqOperator. Then by the name it is clear that both are operators and the first corresponds to the momentum operation while the second corresponds to the momentum squared.

I think it'll be smart for us to keep some convention going forward since it's looking like we're going to have multiple versions of operators that a human would conflate with the same name.
